t: Diagram Interpretation Tool: a plain-language overview
title: Diagram Interpretation Tool: a plain-language overview
description: Overview: what the Diagram Interpretation Tool does and why archives need it. A diagram interpretation tool looks at a picture of a diagram — a flowchart, a circuit sketch, an org chart — and reads it like a person would. It finds the boxes, reads the words inside them, and follows the arrows to learn what connects to what. The picture becomes a structured graph a computer can search and reason about.
demo:
# Diagram Interpretation Tool - runnable demo (JAH-ATK157-000001)
import re
RANK = 1
SIG = False
SAMPLE = 'box start: Begin process\nbox check: Data valid?\nbox done: Store record\nstart -> check\ncheck -> done: yes'
nodes, edges = {}, []
for line in SAMPLE.strip().split("\n"):
    line = line.strip()
    m = re.match(r"box\s+(\w+)\s*:\s*(.+)", line)
    if m: nodes[m.group(1)] = m.group(2).strip(); continue
    m = re.match(r"(\w+)\s*->\s*(\w+)(?:\s*:\s*(.+))?", line)
    if m: edges.append((m.group(1), m.group(2), (m.group(3) or "").strip()))
print("nodes:", len(nodes), "| edges:", len(edges))
for nid, label in nodes.items():
    outs = [e[1] for e in edges if e[0] == nid]
    print(" [%s] %s -> %s" % (nid, label, outs if outs else "(end)"))
if RANK >= 2:
    roots = [n for n in nodes if not any(e[1] == n for e in edges)]
    print("entry points:", roots)
if RANK >= 3:
    labels = " ".join(nodes.values()).lower()
    decisions = [n for n, l in nodes.items() if "?" in l]
    print("decision nodes:", decisions, "| label vocabulary:", len(set(labels.split())))
if SIG:
    print("Signature lineage stamp: JAH-SIG-DIA-" + "JAH-ATK157-000001")
print("record:", "JAH-ATK157-000001", "OK")

t: How the Diagram Interpretation Tool works
title: How the Diagram Interpretation Tool works
description: Overview: what the Diagram Interpretation Tool does and why archives need it. Real diagram readers combine classical vision with text recognition: contour detection and Hough transforms find rectangles, circles, and lines; arrowhead templates identify directed connectors; and OCR reads the labels inside each shape. Each shape becomes a node with its label text, each connector becomes a directed edge, and the result is a graph — nodes, edges, labels — that captures the diagram's meaning. Flowchart symbol shapes (diamonds for decisions, parallelograms for input) add semantic roles on top of the raw geometry.

t: How the Diagram Interpretation Tool works: the deep tour
title: How the Diagram Interpretation Tool works: the deep tour
description: Overview: what the Diagram Interpretation Tool does and why archives need it. Real diagram readers combine classical vision with text recognition: contour detection and Hough transforms find rectangles, circles, and lines; arrowhead templates identify directed connectors; and OCR reads the labels inside each shape. Each shape becomes a node with its label text, each connector becomes a directed edge, and the result is a graph — nodes, edges, labels — that captures the diagram's meaning. Flowchart symbol shapes (diamonds for decisions, parallelograms for input) add semantic roles on top of the raw geometry. Advanced systems train object detectors on annotated diagram corpora to handle hand-drawn and low-quality scans, resolve crossing lines by tracing continuity through junctions, and validate the reconstructed graph against domain rules (every flowchart path should reach an end node). Accuracy is measured by node, edge, and label F1 against human-annotated diagrams. The limits are dense technical drawings where lines overlap heavily and stylized diagrams that break geometric assumptions — those are flagged for human review rather than forced into a wrong graph.

t: The Diagram Interpretation Tool at archive scale
title: The Diagram Interpretation Tool at archive scale
description: Production: how the Diagram Interpretation Tool runs at archive scale and plugs into the extraction pipeline. Real diagram readers combine classical vision with text recognition: contour detection and Hough transforms find rectangles, circles, and lines; arrowhead templates identify directed connectors; and OCR reads the labels inside each shape. Each shape becomes a node with its label text, each connector becomes a directed edge, and the result is a graph — nodes, edges, labels — that captures the diagram's meaning. Flowchart symbol shapes (diamonds for decisions, parallelograms for input) add semantic roles on top of the raw geometry. Advanced systems train object detectors on annotated diagram corpora to handle hand-drawn and low-quality scans, resolve crossing lines by tracing continuity through junctions, and validate the reconstructed graph against domain rules (every flowchart path should reach an end node). Accuracy is measured by node, edge, and label F1 against human-annotated diagrams. The limits are dense technical drawings where lines overlap heavily and stylized diagrams that break geometric assumptions — those are flagged for human review rather than forced into a wrong graph.
